result.topic_en: Euler works through the case m = 4, n = 4 for his double sums. He derives 6ζ(4)² = 7ζ(8) and a value for the sum ∫1/z^7(1/y) (in modern notation ζ(7,1)). He concludes that ∫1/z^5(1/y^3) and ∫1/z^6(1/y^2) can only be found jointly in one linear relation, not separately.
result.transcription:
160 MEDITATIONES CIRCA
$6\int\frac{1}{z^5}\left(\frac{1}{y^3}\right)+15\int\frac{1}{z^6}\left(\frac{1}{y^2}\right)+30\int\frac{1}{z^7}\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)=$
$30\int\frac{1}{z^6}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^2}+\frac{9}{2}\int\frac{1}{z^4}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^4}-\frac{7}{2}\int\frac{1}{z^8}.$
Sit denique $m=4$ et $n=4$, eritque
$\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{1}{z^4}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^4}-\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{1}{z^8}=2\int\frac{1}{z^4}\cdot\frac{1}{z^4}+20\int\frac{1}{z^6}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^2}-\int\frac{1}{z^4}\left(\frac{1}{y^4}\right)-4\int\frac{1}{z^5}\left(\frac{1}{y^3}\right)$
$-10\int\frac{1}{z^6}\left(\frac{1}{y^2}\right)-20\int\frac{1}{z^7}\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)$
hincque
$4\int\frac{1}{z^5}\left(\frac{1}{y^3}\right)+10\int\frac{1}{z^6}\left(\frac{1}{y^2}\right)+20\int\frac{1}{z^7}\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)=20\int\frac{1}{z^6}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^2}+\int\frac{1}{z^4}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^4}$
quae aequatio cum praecedente eandem continet determinationem, ac reducitur ad hanc proprietatem:
$6\int\frac{1}{z^4}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^4}=7\int\frac{1}{z^8}$
quae valoribus a me inuentis $\int\frac{1}{z^4}=\frac{\pi^4}{90}$ [?] et $\int\frac{1}{z^8}=\frac{\pi^8}{9450}$ egregie eſt conformis. Sin autem haec vltima aequatio cum caſu ſecundo conferatur, inde colligitur
$4\int\frac{1}{z^7}\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)=4\int\frac{1}{z^2}\int\frac{1}{z^6}-4\int\frac{1}{z^3}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^5}+8\int\frac{1}{z^4}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^4}-7\int\frac{1}{z^8}$ ſeu
$\int\frac{1}{z^7}\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)=\int\frac{1}{z^2}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^6}-\int\frac{1}{z^3}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^5}+\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{1}{z^4}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^4}$
qui valor cum caſu primo collatus praebet
$2\int\frac{1}{z^2}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^6}+\int\frac{1}{z^4}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^4}=\frac{9}{2}\int\frac{1}{z^8}$
quae aequatio etiam veritati eſt conſentanea. Hinc praeter ſeriem $\int\frac{1}{z^7}\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)$ et determinationes primae methodi, tantum hanc vnicam nouam determinationem conſequimur:
$2\int\frac{1}{z^5}\left(\frac{1}{y^3}\right)+5\int\frac{1}{z^6}\left(\frac{1}{y^2}\right)=10\int\frac{1}{z^3}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^5}-\frac{9}{2}\int\frac{1}{z^4}\cdot\int\frac{1}{z^4}$
neque ergo ſummas harum ſerierum $\int\frac{1}{z^5}\left(\frac{1}{y^3}\right)$ et $\int\frac{1}{z^6}\left(\frac{1}{y^2}\right)$ ſeorſim definire licet.
Ordo

items.quote: quae valoribus a me inuentis $\int\frac{1}{z^4}=\frac{\pi^4}{90}$ [?] et $\int\frac{1}{z^8}=\frac{\pi^8}{9450}$ egregie eſt conformis
items.english: which agrees excellently with the values found by me, ∫1/z^4 = π^4/90 and ∫1/z^8 = π^8/9450.

items.quote: quae aequatio etiam veritati eſt conſentanea
items.english: which equation also agrees with the truth.

items.quote: neque ergo ſummas harum ſerierum $\int\frac{1}{z^5}\left(\frac{1}{y^3}\right)$ et $\int\frac{1}{z^6}\left(\frac{1}{y^2}\right)$ ſeorſim definire licet.
items.english: Therefore the sums of these series ∫1/z^5(1/y^3) and ∫1/z^6(1/y^2) cannot be determined separately.
